books.section: Topic 8.10 The African-American Civil Rights Movement (1960s)
The Civil Rights Movement in the 1960s: From Integration to Black Power

source: original; stimulus is an original account drawn from the grounding books

stimulus.source_note: Account drawn from the grounding books (5 Steps Ch. 27; Princeton Ch. 12; Barron's Ch. 10, Topic 8.10). The June 21, 1964 murder date, the three names, and the Atlantic City compromise are in the books and the standard accounts (Library of Congress and the National Archives on Freedom Summer and the MFDP).
stimulus.text: In the summer of 1964 about a thousand volunteers, most of them white college students from the North, came to Mississippi for Freedom Summer. They joined local Black organizers to register Black voters and to teach in Freedom Schools. On June 21, 1964, three of the workers, James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner, were murdered near Philadelphia, Mississippi, after being arrested and released by local police. Their bodies were found six weeks later. The murders drew national attention to the violence facing Black Mississippians who tried to vote. That August the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party (MFDP), led by sharecropper Fannie Lou Hamer, went to the Democratic National Convention in Atlantic City and asked to be seated as Mississippi's true delegation, since Black Mississippians had been kept from voting in the regular party. The convention offered the MFDP two at-large seats instead, and the MFDP refused them.

stem: Why did Freedom Summer organizers bring white college students from the North to Mississippi?

options.text: Mississippi had no Black organizers willing to register voters there
options.misconception: The passage says the volunteers joined local Black organizers, who were already there.

options.text: Violence against white Northern students would draw national attention to Mississippi
The students were paid by Mississippi to teach in its public schools
options.misconception: The passage says they taught in Freedom Schools, not in Mississippi's public schools, and mentions no pay.

options.text: The students were sent by the Supreme Court to enforce the Brown decision
options.misconception: The passage says nothing about the Supreme Court sending the students.

rationales.A: The passage says the volunteers joined local Black organizers, so Black organizers were already working there.
rationales.B: Background: The organizers brought white Northern students to Mississippi so that violence against them would draw national attention. The passage says the murders drew national attention to the violence facing Black Mississippians.
rationales.C: The volunteers taught in Freedom Schools, not in the state's public schools, and the passage mentions no pay.
rationales.D: No court sent the students; they were volunteers for a voter-registration project.
rationales.general:
1. About a thousand mostly white Northern students join local Black organizers in Mississippi.
2. They register Black voters and teach in Freedom Schools through the summer of 1964.
3. Three workers are murdered, and the murders draw national attention.
4. Background: The attention falls on Mississippi because the victims include white Northern students.
Remember: A protest can borrow attention by bringing in people the press will follow.
